title: Crypto agility: versioned envelopes, negotiation and dual signing
description: Design a self-describing, versioned envelope with algorithm identifiers, one registry and a policy (active / deprecated / disallowed, signature phases) so AES-GCM can become ChaCha20-Poly1305 and Ed25519 can become ML-DSA without a flag day; prove it with a static fitness check.
outcome: You can compare three agility designs with measured evidence, choose one and record it in an ADR, swap an algorithm with a policy change while old data stays readable, negotiate without fallback, dual-sign safely (the verifier's policy decides which signatures are required), and keep the design true with a static check that fails the build on any hard-coded algorithm.
environment: Python 3.12 (3.9+), cryptography==50.0.2 (wheels built with OpenSSL 4.0.3: ML-KEM, ML-DSA, HPKE available), stdlib otherwise
overview: Measure three ways to make a format swappable, decide, then break the chosen design with a seeded signature-stripping attack: the verifier trusted the envelope's own list of signatures. Fix it so policy decides, and add a fitness function that keeps algorithms inside the registry.

glossary.meaning: A short registered name (A256GCM, ML-DSA-65) carried with the data so readers can dispatch to the right code.
The one module that maps identifiers to implementations and a status: active, deprecated (read/verify only) or disallowed.
Which signatures a verifier requires: classic (Ed25519), transition (Ed25519 + ML-DSA-65), pq-only (ML-DSA-65).
Removing one signature of a dual-signed object so a verifier that accepts 'any valid signature' checks only the weaker one.
An automated test that keeps an architectural decision true (here: no algorithm named outside the registry).

concepts: The label names the algorithm; the policy decides if it is acceptable.
Swapping the default is a policy change; old data stays readable until its algorithm is disallowed.
Negotiation fails closed: no common active algorithm = error, never fallback.
Dual signing only helps if the verifier requires both signatures.

designBrief.context: Encrypted, signed invoices are stored for 10 years and read by several services. Ed25519 must give way to ML-DSA (FIPS 204) before quantum attackers arrive, and the AEAD may need replacing after an incident. Today the cipher is implied by the code.
constraints: 0 records rewritten before an algorithm switch (no flag day)
old records stay readable until their algorithm is explicitly disallowed
header overhead <= 64 bytes per envelope
a verifier in the transition phase rejects any envelope missing a required signature
0 hard-coded algorithms outside registry.py (static check in CI)
designBrief.question: How should the envelope name its algorithms, and who decides which algorithms and signatures are acceptable?

options.name: A: one algorithm, no identifier (v1)
options.description: The format version implies AES-256-GCM; no signatures listed.
options.evidence: 1000 rewrites before a switch, or 2.0 trial decryptions per read after it; header 43 B.
options.verdict: Rejected: every change is a flag day and readers must guess.

options.name: B: per-algorithm identifiers + registry + policy (v2)
options.description: Header carries v, aead, kid, nonce, ctx (all AAD); signatures carry their algorithm id; the registry and policy decide.
options.evidence: +31 header bytes (74 B), 0 rewrites, 1000/1000 old documents readable after the switch; dual signature 3373 B.
options.verdict: Chosen (ADR-0017), with the verifier fix from the failure lab.

options.name: C: one suite identifier per combination
options.description: TLS-1.2-style suite ids covering AEAD + signature phase together.
options.evidence: 6 suite ids today vs 4 per-algorithm ids; 9 after adding one AEAD.
options.verdict: Rejected for this format: combinatorial growth (RFC 7696 2.1); fine for protocols that negotiate whole suites.

fitnessFunction.what: No module outside the registry imports a primitive, names an algorithm class or hard-codes an algorithm id (AST check, also run over the capstone).

scalingLimits: Many algorithms in the registry: every entry is a code path to test; signal = registry entries with zero reads in the envelopes_by_aead metric for months (prune them) or entries without a round-trip test.
Very long-lived data: lazy migration on read never touches cold records; signal = deprecated-algorithm counts that stop falling - schedule a background re-seal job like lesson 12's rewrap.

Signature size: dual signing adds 3,373 B per envelope; for millions of small records the signatures dominate storage - signal = signature bytes / payload bytes > 1; sign batches or manifests instead of each record.

codeWalkthrough.title: registry.py
codeWalkthrough.detail: The only module that imports primitives. REGISTRY maps ids to Alg(id, kind, status, impl); PHASES maps a policy phase to required signature ids; get() raises UnknownAlgorithm / DisallowedAlgorithm (for_new_data refuses deprecated).

codeWalkthrough.title: Keyring
codeWalkthrough.detail: Data keys by kid, each bound to exactly one algorithm id; primary() picks the newest key for the policy default.

codeWalkthrough.title: seal
codeWalkthrough.detail: The header {v, aead, kid, n, ctx} is the AEAD's AAD (canonical JSON); signatures are computed over header + ciphertext for every algorithm the policy phase requires (sig_algs lets an attacker choose fewer - the fault).

codeWalkthrough.title: open_
codeWalkthrough.detail: Dispatches on the version: v1 implies LEGACY_V1_AEAD with empty AAD, v2 reads the header; refuses a key/algorithm mismatch; the registry refuses disallowed algorithms.

codeWalkthrough.title: verify (the bug)
codeWalkthrough.detail: any() over listed signatures: an envelope carrying only the classical signature passes. The fix iterates registry.required_signatures() instead.

codeWalkthrough.title: negotiate / migrate
codeWalkthrough.detail: Local preference order, active only, NoCommonAlgorithm instead of fallback; migrate re-seals only envelopes that are legacy or off the default.

codeWalkthrough.title: count_by_aead + agility_lint
codeWalkthrough.detail: The envelopes_by_aead metric tells you when an algorithm can be disallowed; agility_lint (AST) keeps algorithm choices inside the registry.

glossary.meaning: Module-lattice key-encapsulation mechanism: encapsulate(public key) -> (shared secret, ciphertext). ML-KEM-768: 1,184 B public key, 1,088 B ciphertext, 32 B secret.
Module-lattice signature scheme. ML-DSA-65: 1,952 B public key, 3,309 B signature; signing is randomised (hedged) by default.
A post-quantum and a traditional exchange run together; the secrets are concatenated and fed to the KDF, so both must break.
TLS 1.3 group 0x11EC (RFC 10024): client share = ML-KEM pk || X25519 (1,216 B), server share = ML-KEM ct || X25519 (1,120 B).
Record encrypted traffic today; decrypt it once a cryptographically relevant quantum computer exists.

concepts: Key exchange migrates first: recorded traffic is the urgent risk.
Hybrid = secure if either component holds.
Check the share length; abort, never fall back.
PQ signatures cost far more bytes than PQ key exchange.

code:
"""Post-quantum key exchange in practice: X25519, ML-KEM-768 (FIPS 203) and the hybrid X25519MLKEM768 (RFC 10024).
A toy TLS-1.3-shaped exchange: the client sends a key share, the server answers with a share, both derive one key.
Shares and secret order follow RFC 10024: ML-KEM part first, then X25519 (1216 B client share, 1120 B server share)."""
import hashlib
import json
import random

from cryptography.hazmat.primitives import hashes
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.asymmetric import mlkem, x25519
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.kdf.hkdf import HKDF

SEED = 18  # seeds the injected fault (how the attacker rewrites the server share)
GROUP = "X25519MLKEM768"  # IANA TLS group 0x11EC (RFC 10024 section 7.1)
MLKEM_PK, MLKEM_CT, X_LEN = 1184, 1088, 32


class HandshakeError(Exception):
    """Abort the handshake (TLS: illegal_parameter alert) instead of continuing with weaker keys."""


def x_pub(k) -> bytes:
    return k.public_key().public_bytes_raw()


def derive(secret: bytes, client_share: bytes, server_share: bytes) -> bytes:
    transcript = hashlib.sha256(client_share + server_share).digest()  # bind the key to both shares
    return HKDF(hashes.SHA256(), 32, salt=None, info=b"kb-l18 hybrid" + transcript).derive(secret)


def client_hello():
    st = {"mlkem": mlkem.MLKEM768PrivateKey.generate(), "x": x25519.X25519PrivateKey.generate()}
    st["share"] = st["mlkem"].public_key().public_bytes_raw() + x_pub(st["x"])  # 1184 + 32 = 1216 bytes
    return st, st["share"]


def server_respond(client_share: bytes):
    if len(client_share) != MLKEM_PK + X_LEN:
        raise HandshakeError("illegal_parameter: client share length")
    ss_pq, ct = mlkem.MLKEM768PublicKey.from_public_bytes(client_share[:MLKEM_PK]).encapsulate()
    xk = x25519.X25519PrivateKey.generate()
    ss_x = xk.exchange(x25519.X25519PublicKey.from_public_bytes(client_share[MLKEM_PK:]))
    server_share = ct + x_pub(xk)  # 1088 + 32 = 1120 bytes
    return server_share, derive(ss_pq + ss_x, client_share, server_share)  # 64-byte hybrid secret, ML-KEM first


def client_finish(st: dict, server_share: bytes):
    """Returns (key, mode). mode tells which secrets protect the session."""
    if len(server_share) == MLKEM_CT + X_LEN:
        ss_pq = st["mlkem"].decapsulate(server_share[:MLKEM_CT])
        ss_x = st["x"].exchange(x25519.X25519PublicKey.from_public_bytes(server_share[MLKEM_CT:]))
        return derive(ss_pq + ss_x, st["share"], server_share), GROUP
    # BUG on purpose: "be liberal in what you accept" - silently fall back to classical X25519 only
    ss_x = st["x"].exchange(x25519.X25519PublicKey.from_public_bytes(server_share[-X_LEN:]))
    return derive(ss_x, st["share"], server_share), "X25519 (fallback)"


def harvest_then_break(st: dict, server_share: bytes, x_server=None) -> bytes:
    """A future quantum attacker recovers X25519 private keys from recorded traffic (Shor). Can it get the key?"""
    ss_x = st["x"].exchange(x25519.X25519PublicKey.from_public_bytes(server_share[-X_LEN:]))  # X25519 is broken
    return derive(ss_x, st["share"], server_share)  # but it has no ML-KEM shared secret


def sizes() -> dict:
    k = mlkem.MLKEM768PrivateKey.generate()
    k1024 = mlkem.MLKEM1024PrivateKey.generate()
    return {"X25519": {"client_share": 32, "server_share": 32, "secret": 32},
            "ML-KEM-768": {"client_share": len(k.public_key().public_bytes_raw()),
                           "server_share": len(k.public_key().encapsulate()[1]), "secret": 32},
            "ML-KEM-1024": {"client_share": len(k1024.public_key().public_bytes_raw()),
                            "server_share": len(k1024.public_key().encapsulate()[1]), "secret": 32},
            GROUP: {"client_share": MLKEM_PK + X_LEN, "server_share": MLKEM_CT + X_LEN, "secret": 64}}


if __name__ == "__main__":
    rng = random.Random(SEED)
    for name, s in sizes().items():
        print(json.dumps({"kem": name, **s, "on_wire": s["client_share"] + s["server_share"]}))
    st, ch = client_hello()
    sh, k_server = server_respond(ch)
    k_client, mode = client_finish(st, sh)
    print(f"1) hybrid handshake: client share {len(ch)} B, server share {len(sh)} B, keys match: {k_client == k_server}, mode: {mode}")
    print("2) quantum attacker with X25519 broken recovers the key:", harvest_then_break(st, sh) == k_client)
    print("--- fault: an on-path attacker rewrites the server share to its X25519 part only (downgrade)")
    st, ch = client_hello()
    sh, _ = server_respond(ch)
    cut = rng.choice([X_LEN, X_LEN + 1])  # seeded: keep only the classical share (or one stray byte)
    k_client, mode = client_finish(st, sh[-cut:])
    print(f"client accepted a {cut}-byte server share | mode: {mode} | quantum attacker recovers key:",
          harvest_then_break(st, sh[-cut:]) == k_client)

title: Keys in hardware-style storage: PKCS#11, non-exportable keys and key ceremonies
description: Design where a long-term signing key lives: a file, a KMS-style service, or a PKCS#11 token that signs through object handles. A PKCS#11-shaped software token shows sessions, PINs, handles and the CKA_SENSITIVE / CKA_EXTRACTABLE one-way attributes; SoftHSM2 runs the same design for real in CI.
outcome: You can explain PKCS#11 slots, sessions, object handles and attributes, sign through a handle, make keys non-exportable by token policy (not application goodwill), compare file / KMS / HSM storage with measured evidence, run a small key ceremony with a verifiable transcript, and audit a token inventory with a fitness test.
environment: Python 3.12 (3.9+), cryptography==50.0.2 (wheels built with OpenSSL 4.0.3: ML-KEM, ML-DSA, HPKE available), stdlib otherwise; pending CI: SoftHSM2 (Ubuntu softhsm2 / Homebrew softhsm 2.7.0) + python-pkcs11 0.10.1
overview: Measure three storage options under a simulated host compromise, decide, then let a compromised application read a key from a token whose defaults are 'extractable'. Move the decision into the token, prove it with tests, and run a key ceremony.

glossary.meaning: OASIS C API for cryptographic tokens (HSMs, smart cards, SoftHSM): slots, tokens, sessions, objects with attributes, mechanisms (CKM_*).
A number that refers to a key inside the token; the app passes it to C_Sign - the key bytes never leave.
Never reveal the value in plaintext / never allow wrapping it out. One-way: sensitive can only be turned on, extractable only off.
Read-only history: true only if the key was protected for its whole life (generated inside, never exposed).
Scripted, witnessed generation of a long-term key inside the device, ending with a public-key fingerprint and proof of possession.

concepts: The app holds a handle, not a key.
The token enforces non-exportability; templates cannot opt out.
Compromise turns theft into misuse: bounded and logged.
Long-term keys are born in a ceremony.

designBrief.context: The release-signing key (lesson 14) signs every artifact. It sits as a PEM file on the build host. A build-host compromise must not let the attacker sign releases after the incident is cleaned up.
constraints: the application process can never read private key bytes
after clean-up (key disabled / session closed) the attacker can no longer sign
signing latency <= 1 ms on the build host
every signing operation leaves an audit event
recovery plan if the device is lost
designBrief.question: Where should the signing key live and how does the application use it?

options.name: A: PEM file next to the app
options.description: Load the key from disk (optionally password-encrypted; the app can decrypt it).
options.evidence: app can read key: True; sign ≈35.1 µs; attacker signs after clean-up: True.
options.verdict: Rejected: a single read gives permanent signing power.

options.name: B: KMS-style remote signing
options.description: Key stays in a service (OpenBao transit exportable=false, cloud KMS); app sends data to sign.
options.evidence: app can read key: False; sign ≈5001.5 µs over HTTP on 127.0.0.1 (new connection per call); after clean-up: False (key disabled).
options.verdict: Good for many services; misses the 1 ms constraint without connection reuse.

options.name: C: PKCS#11 token, non-exportable, sign via handle
options.description: Key generated inside the token; token policy forces SENSITIVE=True, EXTRACTABLE=False.
options.evidence: app can read key: False; sign ≈40.1 µs; after clean-up: False.
options.verdict: Chosen for the build host (ADR-0019); front with a KMS when many services sign.

fitnessFunction.what: Static: no module outside the token implementation reads private key bytes (private_bytes*, wrap_key). Inventory: every private key on the token is ALWAYS_SENSITIVE and NEVER_EXTRACTABLE. Also run over the capstone.
fitnessFunction.threshold: 0 forbidden calls; 0 exportable private keys in the inventory

scalingLimits: Throughput: one token signs serially; signal = sign queue latency rising with release frequency - add tokens/HSM partitions or batch-sign manifests.
Many consumers: per-host tokens multiply ceremonies and PINs; signal = number of hosts holding signing PINs - centralise behind a KMS (OpenBao transit with external-key) and audit there.
Disaster recovery: non-exportable keys cannot be restored from software backups; signal = a single device holding a production key - provision a second device in the ceremony and rehearse rotation.

title: End-to-end encryption for groups: pairwise, sender keys and MLS-style epochs
description: Compare pairwise fan-out, sender keys and an MLS-style ratchet tree (RFC 9420 ideas: epochs, Commits with fresh entropy, log-sized updates) with measured encryption counts; build a toy epoch-based group key whose removal really excludes the removed member.
outcome: You can explain forward secrecy and post-compromise security for groups, compute what a removal costs in each design at n = 8, 64, 256, implement tree Commits (path secrets to copath resolutions) with HPKE, find and fix the 'forgot to blank the removed path' bug, and keep it fixed with a property-style fitness test.
environment: Python 3.12 (3.9+), cryptography==50.0.2 (wheels built with OpenSSL 4.0.3: ML-KEM, ML-DSA, HPKE available), stdlib otherwise; equivalent (pending CI): OpenMLS (Rust, MIT)
overview: Count real encryptions for three designs, choose the tree, then remove a member with a seeded bug: the removed leaf is blanked but its parent keys are not, so the removed member reads the next epoch. Blank the path, and prove it over every (committer, removed) pair.

glossary.meaning: A period with one group secret known exactly to the current members; every Commit starts a new epoch (RFC 9420).
A message that applies changes (add/remove/update) and injects fresh entropy along the committer's path to the root.
Binary tree of key pairs; the resolution of a node is the smallest set of non-blank nodes covering everyone below it.
Compromise now does not reveal past messages (old epoch keys are deleted).
After a compromised member updates, the attacker loses access to future epochs.

concepts: New epochs need fresh entropy the removed member never receives.
A Commit costs about log2(n) public-key encryptions.
Remove = blank the leaf AND its direct path.
Updates heal compromise; forward secrecy alone does not.

designBrief.context: Project rooms of 8-256 members; people join and leave weekly; the relay server must not read messages; phones get lost.
constraints: a removed member reads nothing sent after removal
a member who updates after a compromise locks the attacker out (PCS)
removal at n=256 costs <= 2*log2(n) public-key encryptions
1 encryption per application message
designBrief.question: Which group-key design meets removal and recovery requirements at 256 members?

options.name: A: pairwise fan-out
options.description: Each message encrypted to each member over pairwise channels.
options.evidence: per message: 255 encryptions at n=256; removal: 0.
options.verdict: Rejected for big rooms: per-message cost grows with n (fine below ~5 members).

options.name: B: sender keys
options.description: Each member distributes a chain key; 1 encryption per message; after removal all remaining members redistribute.
options.verdict: Rejected: removal and PCS scale quadratically (RFC 9420 introduction).

options.name: C: MLS-style tree with epochs
options.description: Commits encrypt fresh path secrets to copath resolutions; removal blanks the removed path.
options.evidence: removal: 4 / 10 / 14 encryptions (1,120 B at 256); removed member can read: False.
options.verdict: Chosen (ADR-0020); production via a reviewed RFC 9420 implementation.

fitnessFunction.what: Seeded random sequence of removals and updates in a 16-member group: after every change exactly the current members read the new epoch, and no commit exceeds the log budget.
fitnessFunction.threshold: 0 leaks to removed members; commit cost <= 2*log2(16) = 8 HPKE encryptions

scalingLimits: Concurrent commits: two committers in one epoch fork the group; signal = decrypt failures clustered by epoch - the delivery service must order commits per group.
Very large groups (thousands): tree blanks from many removals push commit cost towards O(n); signal = commit size growing over time - re-key the whole path with periodic full updates.
Idle members: PCS only arrives when members update; signal = age of each leaf key - require updates on a schedule and remove members who never update (RFC 9420 3.2).

codeWalkthrough.title: kdf / node_key
codeWalkthrough.detail: HKDF-SHA256 with labels ('path', 'node', 'commit', 'epoch', 'init', 'app'); node key pairs are derived from path secrets, so whoever learns a path secret learns the node key.

codeWalkthrough.title: Group.__init__
codeWalkthrough.detail: The creator builds the tree; each member learns only the private keys on its own direct path (a simulated Welcome).

codeWalkthrough.title: _remove (the bug)
codeWalkthrough.detail: Blanks only the removed leaf; the parent keys the removed member knew stay in the tree and appear in resolutions. The fix also blanks the direct path.

codeWalkthrough.title: commit
codeWalkthrough.detail: Fresh path secret at the committer's leaf; for each parent: next secret = kdf(prev, 'path'), new node key, HPKE-encrypt the secret to every node in the copath child's resolution.

codeWalkthrough.title: _process
codeWalkthrough.detail: A member decrypts the one entry addressed to a node it knows, derives the rest of the path upward, and computes the commit secret; stale keys (InvalidTag) are skipped.

codeWalkthrough.title: _advance
codeWalkthrough.detail: epoch_secret = kdf(init_secret || commit_secret); the next init_secret comes from the epoch secret - the removed member has init but no commit secret.

codeWalkthrough.title: send / read
codeWalkthrough.detail: Messages are AEAD-sealed with kdf(epoch_secret, 'app') and bound to the epoch number; old epochs no longer decrypt (forward secrecy in the toy).

title: Threat modelling cryptographic systems: STRIDE, attack trees and tests
description: Model this topic's designs (envelopes and rotation, token signing, TLS/PQ key exchange, keys in a token, group messaging) as a data-flow diagram with trust zones, STRIDE threats, controls and the tests that prove them; compute attack-tree paths over verified controls only; let an agent propose threats that code classifies.
outcome: You can build a DFD with trust boundaries, apply STRIDE per element, map every threat to a control or a recorded acceptance and every control to tests that exist and pass, compute the cheapest attack path, detect model drift in CI, and use a local model as a brainstorming aid whose proposals are judged by code.
environment: Python 3.12 (3.9+), cryptography==50.0.2 (wheels built with OpenSSL 4.0.3: ML-KEM, ML-DSA, HPKE available), stdlib otherwise; agent assist: vendored fake model server (tests) or Ollama via LOCAL_MODEL_URL / LOCAL_MODEL
overview: Compare STRIDE per element, attack trees and agent brainstorming on the topic's real designs, then inject everyday drift (a refactor deletes a test, a SIEM export flow is added) that a name-only checker misses. Harden the checker so controls count only with existing, passing tests.

glossary.meaning: Data-flow diagram: external entities, processes, data stores, flows, and trust boundaries between zones.

Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service, Elevation of privilege - each violates authentication, integrity, accountability, confidentiality, availability or authorisation (OWASP).
Apply only the letters that fit an element type (here: external S,R; process all; store and flow T,I,D).
Attacker goal decomposed into AND/OR steps with costs; a step behind a verified control is closed.
The model no longer matches the system: deleted tests, unmodelled flows.

concepts: A control is only as good as the test that proves it.
Every boundary-crossing flow needs Tampering and Information-disclosure threats.
Attack trees show which control matters most.
Agents propose; code classifies; nothing merges automatically.

every threat has a control or an acceptance that names an ADR
every control names tests that exist and pass (run in CI)
an agent may propose threats but never change the model by itself

title: Capstone: an encrypted document service
description: One service that reuses the whole topic: per-document keys in the versioned envelope (17), KEK rotation with retire-after-rewrap (12) in a KMS behind mutual TLS (9-10), document and audit signatures through non-exportable token handles (19), a hash-chained signed audit log with deterministic anomaly rules, PQ-hybrid sharing via HPKE (18), secrets from files with redacted logs (16), a threat model checked by lesson 21's code, and an agent that only explains anomalies.

designBrief.context: A small company stores signed contracts, lets listed colleagues read them, shares some with external partners, and must later prove who read what. Hosts get compromised; insiders exist; quantum attackers may record shares.
constraints: no plaintext DEK or document in the store; KEK only in the KMS
KMS reachable only with a client certificate from our CA
KEK rotation without re-encrypting data; no KEK retired while records need it
audit log tamper-evident (edit, delete, reorder) and signed with a non-exportable key
external shares quantum-safe (hybrid KEM); deprecated KEM refused for new shares
0 hard-coded algorithms, 0 key-export calls, 0 threat-model problems, 0 secrets in logs
an agent may explain anomalies but never decide
designBrief.question: How do the L100-L400 building blocks fit into one service that meets these constraints, and how do we prove it end to end?

architecture.summary: Users call doc_service.py on the app host. For each document it creates a DEK, seals the document in lesson 17's envelope (AEAD id in the AAD header) and signs it through the token's doc-signing handle (lesson 19). It asks kms.py - a separate component holding lesson 12's versioned KEKs - to wrap the DEK over mutual TLS (lessons 9-10), where the caller's identity is its certificate CN. Every operation, including the KMS's, is appended to a hash-chained audit log signed through the token's audit-log handle; audit.py's rules decide anomalies and agent_explain.py only explains them. External recipients receive the DEK through HPKE ML-KEM-768+X25519 (lesson 18). The token PIN is loaded from a file and the JSON app log passes lesson 16's redaction filter.

code:
"""Capstone: an encrypted document service, end to end on 127.0.0.1 with seeded faults. Prints one JSON line per
milestone and a final scorecard. Deterministic code decides every verdict; the agent only explains anomalies.
Run: python run_capstone.py   (add --real to let a local model explain; tests always use the fake server)."""
import base64
import json
import random
import sys
import tempfile
from pathlib import Path

import paths  # noqa: F401
import agent_explain
import agility_lint
import audit
import kms
import registry as reg
import service
import solution_mtls
import solution_verified
import test_fitness_no_key_export as l19_fitness
from doc_service import open_shared
from secrets_app import scan_log

SEED = 22
HERE = Path(__file__).resolve().parent


def m1_envelope_rotation(ns, rng) -> dict:
    for i in range(1, 7):
        ns.svc.put("alice", f"doc-{i}", f"contract {i}: price {rng.randrange(100, 999)}".encode(), readers=("bob", "mallory"))
        ns.clock.advance(1)
    ns.svc.rotate_kek()
    crash = rng.randrange(1, 4)
    try:
        ns.svc.rewrap(crash_after=crash)  # seeded crash part-way
    except RuntimeError:
        pass
    mixed = ns.svc.records_by_kid()
    try:
        ns.svc.retire(1)
        refused = False
    except PermissionError:
        refused = True
    resumed = ns.svc.rewrap()
    retired = ns.svc.retire(1)["retired"]
    readable = sum(1 for d in ns.svc.docs if ns.svc.get("alice", d).startswith(b"contract"))
    return {"milestone": "M1 envelope + versioned KEK + rotation", "crash_after": crash, "records_by_kid_after_crash": mixed,
            "retire_refused_while_in_use": refused, "resumed": resumed, "retired": retired, "readable": f"{readable}/6",
            "pass": refused and readable == 6}


def m2_mtls(ns) -> dict:
    results = {}
    for name, client in (("no client cert", kms.KMSClient(ns.port, ns.pki, with_cert=False)),
                         ("cert from another CA", kms.KMSClient(ns.port, solution_mtls.make_pki_with_client(ns.work / "rogue", "rogue"), ca_file=ns.pki / "ca.pem"))):
        try:
            client.call("rotate")
            results[name] = "accepted"
        except (OSError, PermissionError) as e:
            results[name] = f"refused ({type(e).__name__})"
    ok = ns.svc.get("bob", "doc-1").startswith(b"contract")
    return {"milestone": "M2 mTLS between doc service and KMS", "doc_service_client": "ok" if ok else "failed", **results,
            "pass": ok and all(v.startswith("refused") for v in results.values())}


def m3_audit(ns, rng) -> tuple:
    for i in range(1, 7):  # insider: mallory reads every document within 30 s
        ns.svc.get("mallory", f"doc-{i}")
        ns.clock.advance(5)
    ns.svc.revoke("admin", "mallory")
    ns.clock.advance(10)
    ns.svc.get("mallory", "doc-2")  # stale ACL cache: still allowed (seeded weakness)
    ns.clock.advance(400)
    try:
        ns.svc.get("mallory", "doc-3")
    except PermissionError:
        pass
    clean = audit.detect(ns.audit.entries, ns.audit_pub)
    tampered = json.loads(json.dumps(ns.audit.entries))  # the attacker works on a copy of the stored log
    victim = rng.randrange(2, len(tampered) - 2)
    tampered[victim]["actor"] = "doc-service/bob"  # attacker blames bob
    del tampered[victim + 2]  # and deletes a later entry
    found = audit.detect(tampered, ns.audit_pub)
    rules = sorted({a["rule"] for a in clean})
    return {"milestone": "M3 signed, hash-chained audit log", "entries": len(ns.audit.entries), "clean_log_anomalies": rules,
            "tampered_at_seq": victim + 1, "tampered_log_findings": sorted({a["rule"] for a in found}),
            "pass": rules == ["access_after_revoke", "unwrap_burst"] and {"bad_signature", "seq_gap", "chain_break"} <= {a["rule"] for a in found}}, found


def m4_pq_sharing(ns) -> dict:
    kem = reg.POLICY["share_kem"]
    recipient = reg.new_recipient(kem)
    package = ns.svc.share("alice", "doc-1", recipient.public_key())
    opened = open_shared(package, recipient).startswith(b"contract")
    old = [a.id for a in reg.REGISTRY.values() if a.kind == "kem" and a.status == "deprecated"][0]
    try:
        reg.share_seal(old, recipient.public_key(), b"k" * 32, b"x")
        refused = False
    except reg.DisallowedAlgorithm:
        refused = True
    return {"milestone": "M4 PQ-hybrid sharing (HPKE)", "kem": kem, "pq": reg.REGISTRY[kem].pq, "recipient_opened": opened,
            "wrapped_dek_bytes": len(base64.b64decode(package["blob"])), f"new_share_with_{old}": "refused" if refused else "allowed",
            "pass": opened and refused and reg.REGISTRY[kem].pq}


def m5_fitness(ns) -> dict:
    ns.log.debug("upstream call", extra={"ctx": {"authorization": "Bearer " + "z" * 24, "pin": ns.pin.reveal()}})  # seeded leak attempt
    checks = {"agility_lint_violations": len(agility_lint.scan([HERE])),
              "key_export_calls": len(l19_fitness.key_export_calls([HERE])),
              "token_keys_exportable": len(l19_fitness.inventory(ns.token)),
              "threat_model_problems": len(solution_verified.check(solution_verified.load(HERE / "threat_model.json"))),
              "secrets_in_logs": len(scan_log(ns.log_stream.getvalue(), known=[ns.pin.reveal()]))}
    return {"milestone": "M5 fitness functions + threat model + secret handling", **checks, "pass": not any(checks.values())}


def m6_agent(anomalies, real=False) -> dict:
    rows = agent_explain.explain(anomalies, real=real)
    verdicts = {r["id"]: r["verdict"].split()[0] for r in rows}
    page = any(a["rule"] in ("bad_signature", "chain_break", "seq_gap") for a in anomalies)  # code decides the action
    return {"milestone": "M6 agent explains, code decides", "anomalies": len(anomalies),
            "accepted": sum(v == "ACCEPTED" for v in verdicts.values()), "rejected": [i for i, v in verdicts.items() if v == "REJECTED"],
            "action": "page on-call (integrity)" if page else "ticket", "pass": all(verdicts.get(a["id"]) for a in anomalies) and "A99" not in [i for i, v in verdicts.items() if v == "ACCEPTED"]}


def run(real=False) -> list:
    rng = random.Random(SEED)
    with tempfile.TemporaryDirectory(dir=HERE, ignore_cleanup_errors=True) as work:
        ns = service.start(Path(work))
        ns.work = Path(work)
        try:
            rows = [m1_envelope_rotation(ns, rng), m2_mtls(ns)]
            m3, anomalies = m3_audit(ns, rng)
            rows += [m3, m4_pq_sharing(ns), m5_fitness(ns), m6_agent(anomalies, real)]
        finally:
            service.stop(ns)
    return rows


if __name__ == "__main__":
    rows = run(real="--real" in sys.argv)
    for row in rows:
        print(json.dumps(row, sort_keys=False))
    print(json.dumps({"scorecard": "capstone", "passed": sum(r["pass"] for r in rows), "total": len(rows), "decided_by": "code"}))

checkYourself.q: Why can the attacker who owns the doc-service host still read documents, and what limits it?
checkYourself.a: It can ask the KMS to unwrap while it is in; the KEK never leaves the KMS and the audit rules flag bursts, so access is bounded and visible.

checkYourself.q: What does the hash chain detect that signatures alone do not?
checkYourself.a: Deletion and reordering: each entry commits to the previous one, so a missing or moved entry breaks the chain and the sequence.

checkYourself.q: Why is the agent's A99 explanation rejected?

conceptSummary: An encrypted document service built from the topic's labs: envelope + registry (17), KEK rotation (12) in a KMS behind mTLS (9-10), signatures through non-exportable token handles (19), a signed hash-chained audit log with rule-based anomalies, PQ-hybrid sharing (18), secret handling (16) and a threat model checked by code (21). Code decides; the agent explains.
inRealSystems: Document and file services (and secrets managers) use exactly this split: envelope encryption with KMS-held KEKs, mTLS between components, append-only signed audit trails.
Cloud object stores encrypt each object with a data key wrapped by a KMS key and log every KMS call - the same audit-and-rotate story.
useWhen: Use this architecture for any service holding confidential documents for years; avoid KEKs in the app process, local file keys for signing, editable logs, and AI that decides security outcomes.
